D-Wave Just Hit a New 52-Week Low, Down 62% in a Year. Is the Selling Overdone? ©Deagreez from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

D-Wave Quantum stock is down 62% in the past year and set a new 52-week low this week. That's a steeper fall than IonQ's 47% but smaller than Rigetti's 71%.

Revenue shrank in the first half of 2026 while bookings jumped 1,120%, and a class action filed in October alleges those bookings came mostly from two older contracts.

Even after the drop, the stock trades at 67x forward sales, and the Street's 2026 revenue estimate needs a far bigger second half.

The selling doesn't look overdone until the third-quarter report, expected in early November, shows systems delivered and bookings turning into revenue.

D-Wave Quantum (QBTS:NASDAQ) had plenty of good headlines this year: federal money, a partnership with AT&T (T), a gate-model simulator in customers' hands. The stock is still down 62% in the past year (through Friday's close), and it set a new 52-week low this week.

Rigetti Computing (RGTI:NASDAQ) is down 71% over the same stretch, and IonQ (IONQ:NYSE) 47%. But D-Wave's own numbers gave investors plenty of reasons to sell.

What exactly happened

In January, D-Wave agreed to buy Quantum Circuits for $550 million: $250 million in cash and $300 million in D-Wave stock.

In May, first-quarter revenue fell 81% from a year earlier, when the year-ago quarter included a system sale. Nine days later, the Commerce Department's letters of intent put $100 million on the table for D-Wave.

In August, second-quarter revenue of $3.08 million missed the $4.03 million analysts expected, with a wider loss than forecast.

In September, D-Wave finalized a CHIPS Act deal worth up to $100 million in exchange for a minority government stake, which means more dilution. Rigetti got a matching deal.

In October, quantum stocks, IonQ and Rigetti included, slid with tech. D-Wave is down 31% in the past month.

That's a lot of headlines for a company that brought in about $5.9 million of revenue in the first half.

The bookings are the whole bull case now

D-Wave's answer to the shrinking top line has been bookings. First-half bookings jumped 1,120% to $35.5 million, and the backlog climbed to $40.7 million.

Consensus calls for $42.5 million of revenue in 2026 and $80.6 million in 2027. From 2022 to 2025, D-Wave's revenue ran between $7 million and $25 million a year.

Shares of AT&T (NYSE:T) fell 8% on Friday after a new report stoked investors' fears of a potentially disruptive encroachment by Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) into the lucrative U.S. wireless market.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

A worrisome new threat

SpaceX is in talks to obtain access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the U.S., according to a report by Bloomberg. The telecommunications infrastructure would serve a crucial role in SpaceX CEO Elon Musk's plan to create a formidable rival to AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile.

During SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 20, chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell said Starlink Mobile's monthly users jumped 37% to over 22 million. The satellite-to-cellular network connects ordinary smartphones to SpaceX's low-Earth orbit constellation.

The space technology titan recently acquired a nationwide portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses that it says "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."

"We will be building out our terrestrial network such that there is broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said.

AT&T won't go down without a fight

SpaceX isn't an adversary to be taken lightly. However, building another nationwide wireless carrier won't be cheap, with costs likely to reach tens of billions of dollars. It's also likely to take time -- and perhaps longer than today's sell-off in AT&T's share price would suggest.

In the meantime, AT&T continues to win new customers. The telecom leader added 379,000 postpaid phone subscribers in the third quarter, along with 442,000 fiber and 327,000 fixed wireless customers.

AT&T's revenue, in turn, rose 5% to $32.3 billion, and management lifted its full-year adjusted earnings guidance to $2.40 per share. Following today's declines, AT&T's stock can be had for less than 9 times its projected 2026 profits.

Moreover, the wireless leader expects its cash profits to grow -- not fall -- in the coming years. AT&T sees its free cash flow rising to over $21 billion in 2028, up from $18 billion this year.

AT&T (NYSE:T), a wireless and fiber telecom services provider, closed at $20.93, down 7.96%. Bloomberg's report on SpaceX's cell-site talks pressured the stock, and investors are now watching wireless competition and capital strategy.
Trading volume reached 84.6M shares, coming in about 88% above its three-month average of 45.1M shares.

How the markets moved today

S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 0.53% to 7,623, and the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) slipped 0.21% to 25,955. In U.S. wireless telecommunications services and fiber broadband, Verizon Communications closed at $44.66, down 1.19%, while T-Mobile US fell 7.71% to $146.54 as concerns about carrier competition remained in focus.

What this means for investors

AT&T stock plunged after Bloomberg reported that Space Exploration Technologies is in negotiations to obtain access to around 80,000 cell sites, presumably to build America's fourth nationwide wireless network.

AT&T and its peers, Verizon and T-Mobile, have long operated on the premise that prospective new competitors would avoid entering the market due to the high likelihood of massive capital costs and low profit margins.

Now, SpaceX is blowing this theory out of the water. Additionally, with satellite coverage supplementing a terrestrial network, it would have a competitive advantage among customers who spend a lot of time in rural areas, likely placing further competitive pressure on AT&T.

These fears have also seemed to overshadow good news for AT&T. In its Oct. 21 earnings report, AT&T beat earnings estimates and raised its 2026 guidance. Additionally, NBT Bancorp bought 91,368 AT&T shares valued at around $2.23 million.

Admittedly, an added competitive challenge does not bode particularly well for AT&T. Nonetheless, AT&T provides a necessary service, and wireless customers tend to be sticky. Moreover, investors can buy AT&T stock now at an 11 P/E ratio and earn a 5.3% dividend yield, suggesting the Friday sell-off of the communication stock might be a buying opportunity.

title: How Low Can Charter Communications Stock Go?
detail:
How Low Can Charter Communications Stock Go?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Charter Communications (CHTR) stock has lost 55.7% over the past twelve months, while the S&P 500 returned 15.1%. After a fall of that size, you may hope the worst is behind it. The broader market rose over that year, however, meaning Charter fell without a market-wide selloff. A broader market decline could still come on top of those losses. So how far has Charter fallen when the whole market turned?

How Far Has Charter Stock Fallen In Market Shocks?

Charter stock fell 53% during the 2022 inflation shock, the worst of these periods, while the S&P 500 fell 24%. That was not its low: the stock has since dropped further below its close on the first day of that shock. Charter has weathered 13 market shocks since it began trading in January 2010. Across those periods, its average fall was 16.6%, compared with 13.5% for the S&P 500.

Charter has not always lagged. The stock fell 11% during the 2025 tariff shock while the S&P 500 fell 19%. In the 2020 COVID-19 crash, Charter fell 31%, a little less than the 34% fall in the S&P 500.

Charter fell in 11 of those shocks and returned to its high for that period in nine of them, with a median wait from the low of 1.2 months. Losses from the 2022 fall and the late-2023 bond yield shock have not been made up. Charter stock's latest close is 82.7% below its close of January 3, 2022.

Charter Is Selling Less Than A Year Ago

Over the twelve months to June 2026, Charter's revenue fell 1.5% from a year earlier to $54.4 billion. Five years before, revenue grew 7.2% in the twelve months to June 2021.

Charter's Video revenue fell 9.4% in fiscal 2025, while Internet revenue, its largest business, grew 1.7%. Profit on those sales has held up: the operating margin was 23.8% over the latest twelve months, compared with 24.5% a year earlier.

Charter also owes far more than its shares are worth. Its debt stood at $96.7 billion at the end of June 2026, before the Cox deal closed. That compares with a market value of $13.4 billion at the October 22 close, based on the share count from before the deal.

What Is Getting Worse At Charter Now?

Charter completed its deal with Cox Communications on August 19, 2026. Second-quarter transition expenses to join the two companies totaled $65 million, and management said on the July 24 call that those costs were coming in a bit higher than expected.

Excluding transition costs, management also expects standalone Charter EBITDA, a measure of cash profit from operations, to decline around 1% in 2026. When an analyst asked on that call why Charter had lowered its EBITDA goal for the year, management pointed to broadband subscribers and revenue per customer, after some customer offers did not work out as well as hoped.

SpaceX Wants Half of America's Cell Towers. AT&T Is Paying the Price ©RiverNorthPhotography from Getty Images Signature metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva

AT&T (T:NYSE) shares fell 5.6% on Friday, October 23, to a more than three-month low after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) is in talks to access at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites for a wireless carrier of its own. T-Mobile (TMUS:NASDAQ) lost 5% and Verizon (VZ:NYSE) slipped 1.6%, according to Reuters. None of the companies has confirmed the talks.

It's the second SpaceX hit in two weeks. On October 9, after SpaceX agreed to buy Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum for a reported $8 billion, AT&T closed down 9.81% and Verizon had its worst day since 2002.

Spectrum Was the Paper Threat. Towers Make It Real.

A carrier needs two things: airwaves, and somewhere to hang the radios. SpaceX has a deal for the first (still pending FCC approval), and the tower talks go after the second. Bloomberg named Crown Castle among the companies SpaceX is talking to.

The scale is what stands out. 80,000 sites would be about half of the 158,500 purpose-built cell towers operating in the U.S. last year, per the Wireless Infrastructure Association, and TD Cowen puts the cost of a nationwide network above $80 billion. That's carrier scale, well beyond a satellite service for dead zones.

Crown Castle (CCI:NYSE) jumped 11.6%. AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile were expected to generate nearly 90% of its 2025 site rental revenue, so SpaceX would be its first new national carrier tenant in years.

AT&T's Estimates Are Rising. Its Multiple Isn't.

Analysts are raising AT&T's numbers, not cutting them. Wall Street now expects $2.40 of normalized EPS for 2026, in line with the guidance AT&T raised on October 21, and $2.93 for 2028. On the day of the report, those estimates stood at $2.34 and $2.90.

The stock has gone the other way. AT&T trades at 8.96x NTM earnings, below its five-year average of 9.11x and down from 9.70x on October 21. That's a 7.6% cut to the multiple since then, while the 2026 estimate rose 2.6%.

The market looks to be pricing longer-term competitive risk even as AT&T's earnings estimates rise.

[IMAGE CREDIT: U.S. Air Force photo by Justin R. Pacheco and Edvin Richardson from Pexels via Canva]

Key Takeaways

SpaceX's connectivity business brought in $5.2 billion in the third quarter, up 69% year over year, which works out to about $21 billion a year.

On SpaceX's Oct. 20 earnings call, Elon Musk said he sees a clear path to connectivity revenue about ten times that size or more.

To get there, Starlink Mobile has to become a real U.S. carrier against AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile, and service on its new spectrum doesn't start until early 2028.

Several hundred billion dollars a year is about what AT&T and Verizon took in combined in 2025, and Musk gave no date for reaching it.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) had a big third quarter for Starlink: connectivity revenue came in at $5.2 billion, up 69% year over year and 22% from the second quarter.

Then Elon Musk raised the bar. On the earnings call, he said:

"I can say we do see a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year in connectivity revenue."

That's a big number. And the path to it runs straight through AT&T (T:NYSE), Verizon (VZ:NYSE) and T-Mobile (TMUS:NASDAQ).

About ten times today's business

Start with the math. $5.2 billion a quarter works out to about $21 billion a year. If "several hundred billion" means $200 billion at the low end, Musk is describing a connectivity business roughly ten times its current size. At $300 billion it's closer to 15x.

Connectivity is growing fast enough that this sounds less wild than it might. Starlink added 1.6 million consumer subscribers in the quarter and reached 13.6 million. Consumer ARPU rose 5% from the second quarter to $69 a month, and enterprise and government revenue grew 91% year over year. Gross margin was 55%, with roughly 3 points of that coming from a one-time benefit.

The Street is already thinking big too. Connectivity's $21 billion pace is close to half of the $45.9 billion analysts expect all of SpaceX to bring in this year. And consensus has the whole company at $249.4 billion by 2028.

These estimates may not include the call yet. Since Musk didn't put a date on his number, I wouldn't expect it to change the next three years of estimates much.

title: SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
detail:
SpaceX Just Made Cell Towers Cool Again. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile Are Paying the Price
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 2:51 PM EDT 5 min read
SPCX
T
TMUS
VZ
CCI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

There were some big moves in telecommunications stocks on Friday. On one hand, shares of cell tower owners Crown Castle (NYSE:CCI) and American Tower (NYSE:AMT) soared, with shares up by about 9% and 4%, respectively, as of midday. On the other hand, the three largest wireless carriers plunged, with Verizon (NYSE:VZ), AT&T (NYSE:T), and T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) all deep in the red.

Both moves are due to one company, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX). On Thursday evening, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to secure at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States as it aims to become the fourth nationwide wireless carrier. For context, 80,000 sites would represent about half of all the purpose-built cell towers in the U.S., so it would be a pretty big move.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

This is the second time in October that SpaceX has sent shockwaves through the telecom industry. First, on Oct. 9, SpaceX agreed to buy $8 billion in low-frequency wireless spectrum, and telecom stocks plunged. So, will SpaceX truly boost the tower companies and cost the telecom leaders money?

Why are the tower companies soaring?

First, a little context on how the cell tower business works. The owner builds a tower and then rents space on it to wireless carriers, typically under long-term leases. Next time you drive by a cell tower, take a look at the top. You'll probably see several rings of transmission equipment, and each of those represents a tenant. Since the tower is already standing, adding tenants produces extra revenue with very little additional cost.

Ever since Sprint was acquired by T-Mobile, the tower industry has essentially had three wireless customers. The majority of Crown Castle's rent comes from AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. A well-capitalized fourth player would mean more tenants per tower.

This is also a notable expansion of SpaceX's plans. Although the company has made its telecom network ambitions known for some time, as recently as August, management described its network as small cells mounted on rooftops (not traditional towers). But without getting too technical, the low-band spectrum it bought makes large towers far more useful, so it makes sense to add them to the plan.

Of course, this isn't the first time a "fourth carrier" has emerged. Just a few years ago, Dish Network signed long-term tower leases to build its own 5G network. To make a long story short, Dish's parent company sold most of its spectrum in 2025 and began shutting down the network. Of course, SpaceX is a far more deep-pocketed tenant and could easily afford to build a nationwide network.
